extracted.intended_audience: general readers, inventors, students, and legal researchers interested in U.S. biological patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes legal standards, case law, examples, and controversies concerning the patentability, scope, and enforcement of biological inventions in the United States. Covers composition and method claims, gene patents, genetically modified organisms, cell lines, and related policy issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility patent rights and term
rubrics_metrics.description: As with all utility patents in the United States, a biological patent provides the patent holder with the right to exclude others from making, using, selling, or importing the claimed invention or discovery in biology for a limited period of time - for patents filed after 1998, 20 years from the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the fundamental exclusionary right conferred by U.S. utility patents and the statutory term for post-1998 filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic patentability requirements (novelty, inventive step/non-obviousness, industrial applicability/utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentability generally requires that a technical solution be (1) new, (2) involve an inventive step, and (3) be industrially applicable / useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These baseline requirements apply to biological inventions as to other technologies; the article lists them as the standard patentability elements used to evaluate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products of nature / isolation doctrine (mere isolation insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Until recently, natural biological substances could be patented in the United States if they were sufficiently 'isolated' from their naturally occurring states. However, the US Supreme Court ruled in 2013 that mere isolation by itself is not sufficient for something to be deemed inventive subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples historically allowed (adrenaline, insulin, vitamin B12, gene patents) may no longer be patent-eligible if they are merely isolated natural products; the Supreme Court's holding is a critical limit on composition claims based solely on isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Man-made / genetically modified organisms are patentable (Chakrabarty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Raw natural material is generally rejected for patent approval by the USPTO. The Court (Diamond v. Chakrabarty, 1980) ruled that as long as the organism is truly 'man-made', such as through genetic engineering, then it is patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genetically modified bacteria, viruses, seeds, plants, cells, and even non-human animals can be patented when they are sufficiently the product of human modification rather than natural occurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of isolated and manipulated cells (including human cells) contingent on transformation/novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolated and manipulated cells — even human cells — can be patented. The U.S. PTO issued patents claiming primate and human embryonic stem cells; immortalized cell lines have been patented (e.g., Moore-related patents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biological material removed from a human can become patentable when it has been studied, manipulated, or 'immortalized' so that it differs functionally from the naturally occurring material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gene patent criteria and limits (isolated sequences, known function; post-Myriad constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: A gene patent is a patent on a specific isolated gene sequence, its chemical composition, the processes for obtaining or using it, or combinations of such claims. Historically, U.S. patents on genes were granted on isolated gene sequences with known functions. In 2013 (Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics), the Supreme Court held that a naturally occurring DNA segment is a product of nature and not patent eligible merely because it has been isolated; synthesized DNA sequences (e.g., cDNA) may still be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims directed to naturally occurring DNA sequences are vulnerable under the product-of-nature doctrine; claims to non-naturally occurring, synthetically created sequences or to methods using sequences may have different fates. The article emphasizes that gene patents have been used to claim isolated sequences, diagnostic uses, and altered sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method and diagnostic claim patentability is distinct and case-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent claims can cover methods (e.g., diagnostic testing or drug screening). In Myriad litigation and related appeals, courts treated composition claims and method claims differently: some drug screening claims were upheld by the Federal Circuit while certain diagnostic claims were found unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method claims (drug screening, diagnostic methods, processes) must be evaluated separately from composition claims — they may be more or less vulnerable depending on statutory subject matter doctrines and case law precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of patent claims: compositions, processes, uses, combinations (including genomes, cell lines, transgenic animals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Biological patents have claimed a wide range of subject matter: isolated compositions, processes for obtaining or using biological material, entire genomes, cell lines, genetically modified organisms (e.g., the Oncomouse), and methods for making recombinant proteins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting or evaluating biological patent claims, consider the claim category (composition, method, use, organism) because different categories are treated differently under patent-eligibility jurisprudence and PTO practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents, licensing, and enforcement affect access and practice (exclusive licenses and enforcement examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive licensing and enforcement of biological patents can restrict who performs tests or uses materials (e.g., Myriad's exclusive testing model), and have driven litigation and controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement choices (exclusive vs nonexclusive licensing) have significant downstream effects on healthcare access, research freedom, and commercialization; these practical/policy outcomes influence disputes and policy debates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy and ethical concerns inform evaluation (biopiracy, anticommons, access to diagnostics/medicines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Controversy over biological patents stems from concerns about expense of patented medicines/diagnostics, genetically modified crops and farmers' rights, patenting of indigenous biological resources (biopiracy), and the 'tragedy of the anticommons' where too many owners can block use of resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These normative and empirical concerns are often cited in evaluating whether particular biological patent policies or practices are desirable and have motivated litigation, legislation, and public debate; they are not strict legal patentability criteria but are important evaluative dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on precedent and litigation history to determine eligibility and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Key court decisions (Parke-Davis v. Mulford; Diamond v. Chakrabarty; Moore litigation; Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics) have materially shaped what biological subject matter is patentable and how claims are interpreted and enforced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis of patentability for biological inventions must account for controlling case law and Federal Circuit/Supreme Court holdings; historical practice (e.g., broad gene patents, stem cell patents) has been modified by later decisions.
